title: A Letter to the Editor(s) About MDMA
subtitle: Which now includes me!
body_html:
I'm pleased to announce I've been appointed to the editorial board of the American Journal Theraputics.

This is a general medical journal, with editor-in-chief Peter Manu, M.D. Dr. Manu, whether he knows it or not, is responsible for the crucial first step leading to my career as an academic—almost single-handedly.

The story is as follows: I was in the midst of my first rotation of residency. Year one, month one. It was at the Zucker Hillside Hospital, a freestanding psychiatric hospital, and we had an internal medicine consultation service. All Psychiatrists spent four months being internal medicine doctors, or up to four months of that could be Pediatrics. In my case, I split it. We also do two months of neurology, before we move along to psychiatry in that first year. Historically, it was an entire year of internal medicine before you got to psychiatry, and I would honestly prefer that still be the case.

Dr. Manu ran that Consult service at the time. Peter Manu is tall, affable, robust. There's nothing slight about him, from his laugh to his stride. He's not unhealthy or obese, he takes appropriate care of himself. He's Romanian. With the accent, which immediately endeared me to him, because my medical school roommate was also Romanian. There is a playfulness, which when combined with seriousness I find highly motivating. He clearly love teaching residents. His area of specialization was the problems that present in psychiatric patients, medically. At a place like Hillside Hospital, a lot of individuals had schizophrenia, and were treated with antipsychotic medications that could have severe side effects, and some of which could be quite rare, it was really important to have somebody around who really understood the difference.

The on-call consultation service included junior doctors like myself, who understood enough of medicine to get by, but didn't have the pattern recognition of somebody like Dr. Manu.

And yet, thousands of cases later, he was still curious. He is still curious. My career as an academic started with a question:

“can we give this patient Clozapine again, as an effort to restore a much better quality of life, if it almost killed him the first time?”

Dr. Manu was familiar with these cases. He knew they were life-threatening adverse effects. Hillside Hospital was the place that brought clozapine to America, and our department chair, at the time, was John Kane, the scientist who ran that remarkable FDA approval trial, for still to this day the most effective medication for schizophrenia. But it had this array of life-threatening side effects.

But his answer? It wasn't what I expected.

“Owen…Deepak.” I was on a vacation with my colleague Deepak Sarpal, and he loved referring to us by us by first names.

He paused.

“Why don't you look into it? Tell me what you find.”

For those of you not in medicine, I'm going to emphasize why this is such a remarkable answer. This guy has seen more cases of life-threatening adverse events from clozapine than maybe anybody else. He's got a hunch. But he's not satisfied with the hunch. He wants to know what the data says. He then did something absolutely mind blowing for a pair of first year residents. He cleared our schedules for the next four days, and let us work on nothing but answer answering this question, by reviewing every single paper publishing literature on the topic of retreat with clozapine after life-threatening adverse event, which is referred to as re-challenge, in the literature.

We present our findings to him, and he asked us to turn this into a paper1, and to submit it for publication. To this day, it's my most cited publication. It was written in a week and accepted for publication less than a month later in schizophrenia bulletin, which is a timeframe I've never replicated.

Deepak went on to run a first episode psychosis program in Pittsburgh, and here I am doing research about the adverse effects of antipsychotics, including Tardive dyskinesia— which clozapine prevents and treats— well over a decade later.

One man's curiosity changed my life.

Today, a letter to the editor, who happens to be Peter Manu in this case, was published in the American Journal of Therapeutics, where I am now also a member of the editorial board, an honor I don't take lightly. Most honors I take pretty lightly, I will briefly mention. Most honors are like “top doctor awards,” which honestly, I could do without. Some, however, those chosen by your colleagues, colleagues you respect? Those, I put more stock in.

I was saddened to have to write the following letter, which I will include the citation of, and a screenshot of, because it is an open access letter, in this otherwise not always open access journal.

My colleague and I wrote a series of reviews last year on the topic of psychedelic medicines. One of them was about MDMA2. Subsequently, a number of papers about MDMA were retracted from other major journals, including papers for referenced. My co-Authors and I struggled with whether to retract our review of all of the data from those publications as well, and eventually chose not to do so.

Our letter to the editor explains why we made this choice3, which is not the same choice every citing author published by a journal made.

The data on MDMA has been tainted by unethical practices on the part of some, but not all, of the investigators. This corrupts the whole endeavor. It's wrong. Science can’t rest on a rotten foundation, and misconduct in research is wretched and rotten to the core. What, then, do we do with data collected from human subjects by unethical investigators—even if only in part?

We—the authors of our reviews—decided to honor the research subjects, who gave willingly of themselves, by letting their data be included along with a warning to those who treat research subjects with anything other than the utmost respect. Our conclusion—MDMA needs more research by independent investigators—we were able to stand behind.

This is one of the more difficult decisions I've had to make as an academic, and I hope to never be in the position of having to make such fraught ethical decisions again. It's a lot easier if we conduct ourselves appropriately the first time.

I’m a bit scared of MDMA studies now—either the compound is fraught? Or does the all the fault lie with the investigators? Or, both—perhaps it’s a problematic compound that requires higher standards of conduct, not more lax standards. People who have taken a “love drug” might have a bias? Shocking, I know. The path from the underground to legitimate treatment runs not through it all over again, but upward. We need ever more rigorous studies by endlessly more buttoned up scientists.

Thank you, Dr. Manu, for teaching me that our curiosity can be healing, and that our Diligence, paired with your penchant for grace, can change the course of many lives.

I'm headed to the SWAAY awards tomorrow. For those who I'll see in San Diego, say hello, and I will attempt to greet you with the same warmth that Dr. Peter Manu greets everyone.

The Frontier Psychiatrists is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

1

Manu, P., Sarpal, D., Muir, O., Kane, J. M., & Correll, C. U. (2012). When can patients with potentially life-threatening adverse effects be rechallenged with clozapine? A systematic review of the published literature. Schizophrenia research, 134(2-3), 180-186.

2

Shinozuka, K., Tabaac, B. J., Arenas, A., Beutler, B. D., Cherian, K., Evans, V. D., ... & Muir, O. S. (2024). Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—3, 4-Methylenedioxy-methamphetamine (MDMA). American Journal of Therapeutics, 31(2), e141-e154.

3

Tabaac, B., Muir, O., & Shinozuka, K. (2022). MDMA-Assisted Psychotherapy Phase 3 Trial Publication Retractions. American Journal of Therapeutics, 10-1097.
